title: Lesson 73 - You Might Have Misunderstood Me

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Ben, I need to ask about the careers evening. The group update says I won’t be joining because my schedule is too full. Did you answer for me?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I replied to Carla, yes, but you might have misunderstood what I meant. I wasn’t trying to make the decision for you.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The observable part is that she asked about my availability and you replied before I had seen the invitation. The effect is that the group now thinks I declined.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: That’s a fair point; however, my message may have been summarized more strongly than I wrote it. I said they shouldn’t count on you and could ask you directly next week.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: You may have intended to leave the choice open, but “don’t count on her” could have sounded like an answer.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I may have phrased that badly. I was trying to reduce pressure because you said last weekend that you needed fewer requests this month.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I did say that. Even so, needing fewer requests doesn’t mean I want someone else to accept or decline them for me.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I agree that I should have asked first. I thought forwarding another request might make you feel responsible for saying yes.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That explains your reasoning, but it doesn’t change the impact. I felt excluded from a decision about my own time and work.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I can see that now. My attempt to protect your time may have taken away the choice I meant to protect.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I also noticed myself thinking, “He must believe I can’t manage my schedule.” That conclusion might have gone beyond the evidence.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I don’t believe that. You could have read the group update as a judgment about your ability to manage your own commitments, especially without seeing my original message.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Maybe. But whatever you intended, the effect reached the group, so I now need to correct the record.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Agreed. A possible objection is that the role may already have been offered to someone else. Even if it has, the wording can still be corrected.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Before we decide what Carla understood, can we compare her question, your reply and the group update word for word?

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Yes. The evidence still supports one clear point: I responded about your availability without getting your permission first.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And it supports another: I inferred a broader belief about me that you hadn’t actually stated.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: I would qualify that by saying your inference was understandable, not irrational. The message created room for it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That distinction helps. I’m responsible for checking my inference; you’re responsible for replying on my behalf without asking.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Let’s read the three messages before we plan the correction. We can separate what was written, what may have been understood and what needs repair now.
